title: What does being a woman matter
hookLine: Mara says women lack the wisdom; the nun Soma says it's the mind that matters (SN 5.2)

lines: ALONE IN THE BLIND MEN'S GROVE.
A VOICE: NOT FOR A WOMAN.
cards: The nun Soma has walked out of Savatthi after her meal, into a grove called the Blind Men's Grove, and sat down under a tree for the day's meditation. Then a voice.
Mara, the texts say, wanting to make her afraid and knock her out of her concentration. He doesn't threaten her body.
He goes for something sharper: the state the great sages reach is hard to attain, and no woman, with her little wisdom, can get there. You've probably heard a version of that voice.

teach.b: Mara's words in SN 5.2 are blunt: that place is hard to reach, and a woman can't attain it, with her two-finger wisdom.
Later commentators explain the phrase as a jab at cooking: women testing whether rice was done by pressing a grain between two fingers. Kitchen smarts, not the real thing.
Soma knows exactly who's speaking, and answers in a verse, paraphrased here.

teach.h: WHEN THE MIND IS WELL SETTLED
teach.b: What does being a woman matter, when the mind is well settled, when knowledge is steadily present, when one sees clearly into the Dhamma? Then a line that turns the insult inside out.

teach.h: I AM A WOMAN, I AM A MAN, I AM ANYTHING
teach.b: Anyone who thinks, I am a woman, or I am a man, or I am anything at all, that's the one Mara should talk to.
Notice how she answers. She doesn't argue that women are smarter, or take the bait about kitchens.
She points to the mind, the only thing that matters here, then goes deeper: the sense of being a something, any something, is where Mara gets his grip.
And the refrain: Mara, realizing the nun Soma knows me, sad and disappointed, disappears right there.
This chapter, the Bhikkhuni Samyutta, is ten scenes like this: ten nuns, each alone, each confronted, each recognizing Mara and answering in her own verse.
It's one of the places in the early texts where women speak for themselves about awakening, and they are not shy about it.

how: Buddhist communities read the verses of the early nuns, in the Bhikkhuni Samyutta and the Therigatha, as some of the oldest recorded voices of women on the spiritual path, and Soma's reply is often recited and taught.

o: a woman's duty to her family

p: one who thinks I am anything

s: Soma argues that women are wiser than men
she points to the settled mind, and then past the very idea of being a woman or a man.
the Bhikkhuni Samyutta has ten nuns each answering Mara
ten scenes, ten nuns, each recognizing him and replying in verse.
the two-finger jab is explained by later commentators
they read it as women testing rice between two fingers: kitchen smarts.

games.q: you're Soma, meditating alone. a voice says no woman, with her little wisdom, can reach the goal. what do you do?
o: leave the grove; maybe the voice is right.
argue that women are wiser than men.
recognize Mara, and answer that the settled mind is what matters.
games.why: Soma recognizes him, answers that being a woman doesn't matter when the mind is settled, and Mara disappears.

practice: Let one belittling voice come to mind, from someone else or from inside your own head, you're too old for this, you'll never get it, and hear it once, clearly.

Then, like Soma, don't argue; bring your attention to the breath, the settled body, the mind that's here right now, and let the voice talk to the empty air. If it returns, recognize it again and come back.

wordCard.voice: Itthibhava. The Pali word for being a woman, in the nun Soma's answer to Mara in SN 5.2: when the mind is settled and sees clearly, being a woman, a man, or anything at all is beside the point. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali itthibhava: womanhood, being a woman, the word in Soma's question.

carryVoice: Your line: what does it matter. A settled mind is what this path asks for, in anyone. Day six hundred forty-three, done.
